entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To contact someone again about something you discussed or asked for earlier, to check progress or get an answer.
entries.usage: Very common in work emails: *I'm following up on my email from last week*. Use *on* for the topic and *with* for the person (*follow up with the client on the contract*). The verb is two words, but the noun and adjective are hyphenated: *a follow-up*, *a follow-up email*.
entries.pattern: follow up (with someone) (on something)
examples: I'm **following up on** my email from last Tuesday about the open position on your team.
The nurse will **follow up with** you next week to see how the new medication is working.
Did you ever **follow up on** that apartment listing, or did someone else get it?

drill.sentence: I haven't heard back from the landlord about the leak, so I'll {{follow up}} with him tomorrow.
drill.hint: contact him again about it (not *check in* or *touch base*)

entries.related: *check in* — contact someone to see how things are; *chase someone up* — British, press someone for a reply; *touch base* — brief contact, informal US.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To add someone to a conversation, email thread or project so that they get the information and can take part.
entries.usage: Common in American work email and chat, often as the first line when you add a new person to the cc line, so they know why they're there: *Looping in Maria, who handles billing*. It is informal but widely accepted. In a formal email, write *I've copied Maria*.
entries.pattern: loop someone in / looping in + name
examples: **Looping in** Dr. Patel, who can answer your question about the lab schedule.
I'll **loop** our lawyer **in** before we sign anything.
Thanks for **looping me in**; I hadn't heard that the venue changed.

drill.sentence: I'm not the right person for this, but I'm {{looping in}} Jess from IT, who can reset your account.
drill.hint: adding her to the email — informal (not *copying*, *cc'ing* or *bringing in*)

entries.related: *cc someone* — copy them on an email; *keep someone in the loop* — keep someone informed over time; *bring someone in* — involve them in a project.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep someone informed about a situation or project as it develops, so that they always know the latest news.
entries.usage: Very common in work emails and conversation, as a request or a promise: *Please keep me in the loop*. *Out of the loop* means not informed, often with a feeling of being left out. It sounds friendly and cooperative and is fine in most work emails.
entries.pattern: keep someone in the loop (on / about something)
examples: Please **keep me in the loop** on the contract talks; I need to know before anything is signed.
My brother never **keeps us in the loop**, so we found out about his engagement on Instagram.
The surgeon's assistant **kept the family in the loop** with text updates during the operation.

drill.sentence: I'll be at the conference all week, but please {{keep me in the loop}} if the client changes the deadline.
drill.hint: make sure I stay informed (not *… posted* or *… updated*)

entries.related: *keep someone posted* — give regular updates, informal; *out of the loop* — not informed; *loop someone in* — add someone to a conversation.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To point out something, such as a problem, risk or deadline, so that the right person notices it and can deal with it.
entries.usage: Very common in work emails and meetings: *I just wanted to flag that the room is double-booked*. It sounds helpful and neutral, not like a complaint, so it is a good way to raise a problem with a manager. Common patterns are *flag something to / for someone* and *flag that* + clause.
entries.pattern: flag something (to / for someone) / flag that …
examples: I wanted to **flag** that the invoice uses last year's rates, so the total is wrong.
The pharmacist **flagged** a possible interaction between my two prescriptions.
Our bank **flagged** the purchase as suspicious and froze my card while I was abroad.

drill.sentence: Before you send the report, I should {{flag}} that two of the charts still show the old numbers.
drill.hint: bring this to your attention — one-word verb (not *mention* or *note*)

entries.related: *point out* — plainer; *raise* — bring up an issue for discussion; *a red flag* — a warning sign.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short warning or piece of advance notice, so that someone can prepare for something.
entries.usage: Very common in work emails, chat and speech: *Just a heads-up, the server will be down tonight*, or *Thanks for the heads-up*. It is informal but acceptable in most work emails. The noun has a hyphen; *Heads up!* without a hyphen is a shouted warning to look out.
entries.pattern: give someone a heads-up (about / that …); thanks for the heads-up
examples: Just **a heads-up**: the parking garage will be closed all day Friday, so plan to take the bus.
Thanks for **the heads-up** about the traffic; I took the back roads and made it on time.
The hospital gave staff **a heads-up** that the system update would start at midnight.

drill.sentence: If you're going to be late for dinner, could you at least give me {{a heads-up}}?
drill.hint: advance warning — informal noun with a hyphen (not *a warning*, *a call* or *some notice*)

entries.related: *advance notice* — more formal; *FYI* — information, often with no action needed; *a word of warning* — a warning about a risk.

entries.label: noun (office jargon)
entries.meaning: In office jargon, the time, energy or mental capacity that a person or team has available to take on more work.
entries.usage: Common in tech and corporate settings, usually in the negative: *I don't have the bandwidth for this right now*. It is a polite, slightly impersonal way to say no, but many people mock it as jargon. With clients or in formal writing, say *time* or *capacity*.
entries.pattern: have (the) bandwidth for something / to do something
examples: I'd love to help with the conference, but I don't have the **bandwidth** until my grant is submitted.
With a newborn at home, we just don't have the **bandwidth** to host Thanksgiving this year.
The clinic doesn't have the **bandwidth** to take new patients until it hires another doctor.

drill.sentence: My team is already stretched thin, so we don't have the {{bandwidth}} to take on another client this quarter.
drill.hint: spare time and energy — tech-office jargon (not *capacity*)

entries.related: *capacity* — more neutral, common in management; *have a lot on my plate* — be very busy; *spread too thin* — trying to do too much.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: From now on; in the future, as opposed to what has happened so far.
entries.usage: Very common in business emails, often to announce a change in procedure: *Going forward, please submit all requests through the portal*. It sounds corporate, and after a mistake it can read like a polite criticism of what happened before. In everyday speech, *from now on* is more natural.
examples: **Going forward**, please send all expense reports to Linda instead of me.
The school says that, **going forward**, phones must stay in lockers during class.
We've agreed that, **going forward**, whoever cooks doesn't have to do the dishes.

drill.sentence: The old form caused a lot of errors, so {{going forward}} we'll only accept online applications.
drill.hint: starting now and in the future — business style (not *from now on* or *moving …*)

entries.related: *from now on* — plainer, everyday; *moving forward* — same, also corporate; *in the future* — more general.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, light way to ask someone for an update or a reply, often after they haven't answered.
entries.usage: A standard opening for a follow-up email: *Just checking in on the invoice I sent last week*. The word *just* softens it so it doesn't feel like pressure, though by the third time it starts to. Friends also use it warmly to ask how someone is (*Just checking in, how are you feeling?*).
entries.pattern: just checking in (on / about something / to see if …)
examples: Hi Dana, **just checking in** to see if you had a chance to look at the proposal.
**Just checking in**: did the plumber ever come by to fix the sink?
I'm **just checking in** about the reference letter, since the deadline is this Friday.

drill.sentence: Hi Professor Lee, {{just checking in}} on my request for an extension; I know it's a busy week.
drill.hint: a light way to ask for an update (not *… following up*)

entries.related: *following up* — a little more formal and direct; *touch base* — brief contact, informal US; *a gentle reminder* — politely reminds someone of a task.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, friendly way to say you are willing to help; more generally, *happy to* + verb means you are willing to do something.
entries.usage: Common in emails and customer service, both as an offer (*Happy to help if you need anything else*) and as a reply to thanks. *Happy to* signals willingness, not real happiness, as in *I'm happy to share the slides*. In customer service it can sound scripted, so a specific offer sounds warmer.
entries.pattern: (I'm) happy to help / happy to + verb
examples: If you have any trouble with the new login, let me know; I'm **happy to help**.
"Thanks for watching the kids last night." "**Happy to help**. They were angels."
I'm **happy to share** my slides with anyone who missed the talk.

drill.sentence: "Thanks for explaining the insurance forms." "No problem, {{happy to help}}."
drill.hint: I was willing to assist (not *glad to …* or *my pleasure*)

entries.related: *glad to help* — same; *my pleasure* — warmer reply to thanks; *no problem* — casual reply to thanks.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To contact someone, often for the first time or because you need something, by email, phone or message.
entries.usage: Very common in American business email: *I'm reaching out to ask whether…*, *Feel free to reach out with questions*. It sounds warmer than *contact*, but some people find it overused. It is also used for offering support (*Reach out if you need to talk*).
entries.pattern: reach out (to someone) (about / with something)
examples: I'm **reaching out** because I read your article on urban heat and had a few questions.
If anything changes with your flight, please **reach out to** our travel desk.
After her divorce, several old friends **reached out** to see how she was doing.

drill.sentence: A former colleague {{reached out}} on LinkedIn to ask if I'd be interested in a job at her company.
drill.hint: made contact — common American business verb (not *got in touch* or *wrote*)

entries.related: *contact* — neutral, more formal; *get in touch* — common in both US and UK; *touch base* — check in briefly.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A closing line that thanks someone for help they haven't given yet, because you expect them to give it.
entries.usage: Common at the end of request emails: *Thanks in advance for your help*. Some readers find it pushy, because it assumes the person will agree; *Thanks for considering this* or *Any help would be appreciated* is softer. In casual messages it is sometimes shortened to *TIA*.
examples: Could you send me the final budget by Thursday? **Thanks in advance**!
**Thanks in advance** for taking a look at my résumé; I know you're busy.
Our neighbors' note said they were having a party Saturday and **thanked us in advance** for our patience.

drill.sentence: Could someone on the team cover my shift next Monday? {{Thanks in advance}}, and I'll return the favor.
drill.hint: gratitude expressed before the favor happens (not a plain *thank you*)

entries.related: *thanks for considering this* — softer; *I appreciate your help* — more formal; *TIA* — informal abbreviation.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite opening line when you reply to an email or message later than you should have.
entries.usage: Common at the start of work emails, as a short phrase without a verb. *Sorry for the delay* is more personal and casual, and *Apologies for the late reply* means the same. Avoid long excuses afterward; one short reason, or none, is enough.
examples: **Apologies for the delay**; I was out sick most of last week. Here are the files you asked for.
Hi Ms. Carter, **apologies for the delay** in getting back to you about the apartment; it's still available.
I start almost every email with "**Apologies for the delay**," even when I've only taken a day to answer.

drill.sentence: Hi Tom, {{apologies for the delay}}; your message got buried in my inbox during the move.
drill.hint: polite, verbless way to say sorry for replying late (not *sorry for …* or *… the late reply*)

entries.related: *sorry for the delay* — warmer, more casual; *thanks for your patience* — focuses on the reader instead of your fault; *belated* — late (*belated thanks*).

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: On my side of a shared task, call or process; regarding my part, my equipment or my situation.
entries.usage: Very common in American work chat, email and calls: *Everything looks fine on my end*, *Is it a problem on my end?* It is typical for tech trouble on calls and for saying your part is done. *On your end* and *on their end* work the same way; British speakers more often say *at my end*.
entries.pattern: on my / your / their end
examples: The video is frozen. Is it a problem **on my end** or yours?
Everything's ready **on my end**; I just need your signature to submit the form.
No updates **on my end**, but the moving company said they'd call by noon.

drill.sentence: I tested the link and it works fine {{on my end}}, so maybe try another browser?
drill.hint: regarding my setup — informal US (not *for me* or *on my side*)

entries.related: *on my side* — similar, more neutral; *at my end* — more British; *on your end* — regarding the other person's side.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To send someone a short message, by chat, text or email, usually to ask a quick question or remind them of something.
entries.usage: Very common in tech and office culture: *I'll ping you when it's ready*, *Ping me if you need anything*. It suggests a quick, low-effort message, so it is friendly but too casual for formal emails. *Ping* also works as a noun (*Send me a ping*).
entries.pattern: ping someone (about something / on Slack)
examples: I'll **ping** you on Slack as soon as the slides are ready.
If the baby falls asleep early, **ping** me and I'll come over.
My landlord **pinged** me this morning to say the plumber is coming at ten.

drill.sentence: I'm in back-to-back meetings until four, but feel free to {{ping}} me on Slack if it's urgent.
drill.hint: send a quick message — tech-office verb (not *message* or *DM*)

entries.related: *shoot someone a message* — similar, informal; *DM someone* — send a private message; *nudge* — remind someone gently.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: A deadline meaning by the end of today's working day, usually around 5 or 6 p.m.
entries.usage: Common in American office email and chat, usually read as letters: *Can you send it by EOD?* It can be vague across time zones, so add a time when it matters (*by 5 p.m. Eastern*). *EOW* means end of week, and *COB* (close of business) is a more formal relative.
entries.pattern: by EOD / EOD + day (EOD Thursday)
examples: Can you send me the signed contract by **EOD**? Legal needs it first thing tomorrow.
The landlord texted that the heat would be fixed by **EOD**, but nobody showed up.
I'll have comments on your draft to you **EOD** Thursday.

drill.sentence: The client needs the revised quote today, so please send it to me by {{EOD}}.
drill.hint: abbreviation: the end of today's workday (not *COB*)

entries.related: *COB* — close of business, more formal; *EOW* — end of week; *ASAP* — as soon as possible, no fixed time.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To send someone a quick, short email, without much effort or formality.
entries.usage: Common in American speech and casual email: *Shoot me an email and I'll take a look*. *Shoot* makes it sound fast and easy, and you can also *shoot someone a text* or *a quick note*. Avoid it in formal letters, where it sounds too casual.
entries.pattern: shoot someone a (quick) email / text / note
examples: If you want the recipe, **shoot me an email** and I'll send it tonight.
I'll **shoot the vendor an email** this afternoon to confirm the delivery date.
My advisor told me to **shoot her an email** before dropping by her office.

drill.sentence: I don't have the address on me, but {{shoot me an email}} and I'll send it as soon as I get home.
drill.hint: send me a quick message — casual US verb (not *send* or *drop me a line*)

entries.related: *drop someone a line* — write briefly, a bit old-fashioned; *ping someone* — send a quick message, often in chat; *send someone a note* — neutral.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep giving someone updates about how something is developing.
entries.usage: Very common at the end of emails and conversations: *Keep me posted!* or *I'll keep you posted*. It is warm and informal, fine with colleagues and friends; in formal emails, *please keep me informed* is safer. Compared with *keep someone in the loop*, it is more about receiving news than about being included in a group.
entries.pattern: keep someone posted (on / about something)
examples: Good luck with the interview tomorrow, and **keep me posted**!
The vet said she'll **keep us posted** on how Max recovers from the surgery.
We're still waiting to hear about the permit, but I'll **keep you posted**.

drill.sentence: I hope your mom's appointment goes well. Please {{keep me posted}} on what the doctor says.
drill.hint: send me updates as things develop (not *let me know* or *… updated*)

entries.related: *keep someone in the loop* — keep someone informed, often as part of a group; *keep someone updated* — same, slightly more formal; *let someone know* — tell them once.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly closing line after you give someone information, an answer or advice.
entries.usage: Common at the end of emails, forum answers and chat replies: *Hope that helps!* It sounds warm and modest, as if the answer might not cover everything. *Hope this helps* is just as common, and dropping the *I* is typical of casual writing.
examples: **Hope that helps**! If not, Ravi in accounting knows the system better than I do.
So that's how I'd set up the spreadsheet. **Hope this helps**, and let me know if you get stuck.
I attached last year's packing list for the camping trip. **Hope that helps**!

drill.sentence: The form is on page three of the handbook, under "Leave." {{Hope that helps}}!
drill.hint: friendly closing after giving information (with *that*, not *this*)

entries.related: *let me know if you have questions* — invites a reply; *happy to help* — offers more help; *hope this makes sense* — checks that an explanation was clear.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite invitation meaning you are welcome to do something and don't need to ask permission.
entries.usage: Very common in emails and instructions: *Feel free to reach out with any questions*. It sounds open and friendly; *Please do not hesitate to contact me* is the more formal, old-fashioned version. It invites rather than requires, so avoid it for real obligations: *Please send it by Friday*, not *Feel free to send it by Friday*.
entries.pattern: feel free to + verb
examples: **Feel free to** call me on my cell if you get lost on the way to the office.
There's plenty of food, so **feel free to** bring a friend.
The professor told us to **feel free to** use any programming language for the final project.

drill.sentence: The guest room is all yours, so {{feel free to}} help yourself to anything in the fridge.
drill.hint: you have permission to, without asking (not *please* or *you're welcome to*)

entries.related: *don't hesitate to* — more formal, common in emails; *you're welcome to* — same, slightly warmer; *help yourself* — take food or things freely.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A short, friendly reply meaning *I will do that*, used to agree to a request.
entries.usage: Common in chat, texts and quick emails as an answer to a request (*Can you lock up?* — *Will do!*). It is informal and positive; to a client or in a formal email, write *I'll take care of it*. It usually stands alone or with *thanks* (*Will do, thanks!*).
examples: "Can you send me the slides after the meeting?" "**Will do**. I'll email them tonight."
"Text me when you get home." "**Will do**, Mom."
My landlord asked me to move my bike out of the hallway, so I texted back, "**Will do**!"

drill.sentence: "Could you lock the back door when you leave?" "{{Will do}}, no problem."
drill.hint: short for *I'll take care of that* — two words (not *sure thing* or *got it*)

entries.related: *sure thing* — friendly yes, US; *on it* — I'm starting now, informal; *noted* — I've read it, more neutral.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To send someone a direct, private message on a social media or chat platform, instead of posting in a public or group space.
entries.usage: It comes from social media but is now common at work on Slack or Teams: *DM me if you want the details*. It is also a noun (*send me a DM*), and the past tense is written *DM'd* or *DMed*. Use it when moving a conversation out of a group channel, for example for something personal.
entries.pattern: DM someone (about something); send someone a DM
examples: Rather than post your salary question in the team channel, **DM** me and we can talk.
A stranger **DM'd** my sister on Instagram, claiming she'd won a free phone.
The coach **DMs** each player the practice schedule instead of posting it in the group chat.

drill.sentence: Please don't reply-all with your shirt sizes; just {{DM}} me on Slack.
drill.hint: send me a private message — two letters (not *ping*)

entries.related: *ping someone* — send a short message, public or private; *slide into someone's DMs* — message someone, often flirtatiously; *a group chat* — a shared conversation.

entries.label: email sign-off
entries.meaning: The most common neutral sign-off in American work emails, short for *Best regards* or *Best wishes*.
entries.usage: Safe for almost any work email, from colleagues to people you don't know well. *Best regards* is slightly more formal, *Thanks* more casual, and *Cheers* is used by some Americans but still sounds British to many. Put a comma after it and your name on the next line.
examples: Thanks again for the introduction; I'll let you know how the call goes. **Best**, Jordan
Most of my emails end with "**Best**," because "Sincerely" feels too stiff for coworkers.
My dad still signs his texts "**Best**, Dad," as if he were writing a business letter.

drill.sentence: See you at the workshop on Monday. {{Best}}, Elena
drill.hint: the standard neutral American sign-off — one word (not *Thanks*, *Regards* or *Cheers*)

entries.related: *Best regards* — slightly more formal; *Thanks* — casual, when you've asked for something; *Sincerely* — formal letters and cover letters.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite note reminding someone about a task, deadline or event they may have forgotten.
entries.usage: Common in email subject lines and opening lines: *Just a gentle reminder that forms are due Friday*. *Gentle* softens the message, but a series of gentle reminders can sound passive-aggressive. In American offices, *friendly reminder* is at least as common and works the same way.
entries.pattern: (just) a gentle reminder that … / about …
examples: **A gentle reminder** that timesheets are due by noon tomorrow.
The dentist's office sent **a gentle reminder** about my cleaning on Thursday.
My roommate left **a gentle reminder** on the fridge: "Whose turn is it to buy milk?"

drill.sentence: Hi all, just {{a gentle reminder}} that the lab will be closed on Monday for the holiday.
drill.hint: a soft, polite nudge (not *a friendly …* or *a quick …*)

entries.related: *a friendly reminder* — same, very common in the US; *a nudge* — an informal reminder; *per my last email* — a much sharper reminder.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal email phrase meaning *as we discussed*, used to refer back to an earlier talk.
entries.usage: Common in American business email, often as the opening: *Per our conversation, I've attached the revised quote*. It sounds efficient and official; *As we discussed* is warmer and more common in everyday work. In the related *as per your request*, some editors call *as* unnecessary; *per your request* is enough.
entries.pattern: per our conversation / discussion / call (on + day)
examples: **Per our conversation** this morning, I've moved the launch to the first week of May.
I'm writing, **per our conversation**, to confirm the dates for your daughter's surgery.
The contractor's email began "**Per our conversation**" and then listed costs we had never discussed.

drill.sentence: {{Per our conversation}} yesterday, I'm sending the updated contract with the changes we agreed on.
drill.hint: formal reference back to the talk, with a Latin preposition (not *As per …*, *As discussed* or *Following …*)

entries.related: *as we discussed* — warmer, very common; *per my last email* — often passive-aggressive; *further to our conversation* — the British formal equivalent.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: As soon as you can; a formal phrase that politely but firmly asks for a quick action or reply.
entries.usage: Common in formal letters and in legal and administrative emails: *Please return the signed form at your earliest convenience*. Despite the word *convenience*, it usually means *soon*, and it can sound stiff or insistent. In friendly work emails, *when you get a chance* (relaxed) or *by Friday* (clear) often works better.
examples: Please return the signed consent form **at your earliest convenience** so we can schedule the procedure.
The landlord asked us to call him **at our earliest convenience** about the water damage.
Please RSVP **at your earliest convenience**, since seating at the dinner is limited.

drill.sentence: We are missing one page of your application; please send it {{at your earliest convenience}}.
drill.hint: formal: as soon as you can (not *as soon as possible*)

entries.related: *as soon as possible* — plainer and more direct; *when you get a chance* — relaxed, not urgent; *in a timely manner* — promptly, formal.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short time between receiving a piece of work or a request and finishing it and sending it back.
entries.usage: Common in business, publishing and academia: *Sorry for the quick turnaround*, *We need a quick turnaround on this*. Asking for a quick turnaround is a polite way to say a task is urgent, and it is good manners to acknowledge the pressure. *Turnaround time* is the standard term for how long a process takes.
entries.pattern: a quick / fast / tight turnaround (on something)
examples: Sorry for **the quick turnaround**, but could you review the slides by tomorrow morning?
The print shop is known for **a quick turnaround**: you can pick up flyers the same day.
The journal promises **a quick turnaround** on short papers, usually about three weeks.

drill.sentence: The printer needs the final design by Thursday, which is {{a quick turnaround}} for a whole new logo.
drill.hint: a short time to finish and return work (not *a tight …* or *a fast …*)

entries.related: *a tight deadline* — a deadline that's hard to meet; *a rush job* — work done fast, sometimes badly; *turnaround time* — how long a process takes.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To reply to an older message or thread, often with a short note, so that it moves back to the top of someone's inbox or chat.
entries.usage: Common in email, Slack and online forums when nobody has answered: *Bumping this to the top of your inbox*. It is a light, informal way to remind someone, and a one-line reply like *Gently bumping this* is enough. Bumping the same thread again and again starts to feel pushy.
entries.pattern: bump a / the thread; bumping this (up)
examples: **Bumping this** to the top of your inbox in case it got lost over the holidays.
Nobody answered my question about used cribs, so I **bumped the thread** on the parents' forum.
I **bumped the thread** in the team channel because the server outage still hasn't been explained.

drill.sentence: Since no one replied to my question about the shared freezer, I {{bumped the thread}} this morning.
drill.hint: replied so the old messages rose to the top again (not *revived …*)

entries.related: *follow up* — contact again, more formal; *a gentle reminder* — polite reminder; *resurface* — bring something back to attention.

entries.label: noun (business jargon)
entries.meaning: In business jargon, the request someone is making, such as what they want you to do, give or approve.
entries.usage: Common in American corporate and fundraising talk: *So what's the ask?* or *The ask is two more engineers*. Many people dislike it as jargon for *request*, so avoid it in formal writing. *A big ask* (a lot to request) is common in both British and American English.
entries.pattern: What's the ask? / The ask is …; a big ask
examples: Before you pitch the idea to the director, be clear about **the ask**: money, people, or just approval?
The charity's letter was moving, but **the ask** was buried in the last paragraph.
Five extra hours a week is **a big ask** for volunteers who already have full-time jobs.

drill.sentence: Your email explains the background well, but what exactly is {{the ask}}? Do you need funding or just feedback?
drill.hint: what you want from us — jargon noun (not *the request*)

entries.related: *request* — the neutral word; *a big ask* — a lot to request; *the pitch* — the presentation that leads up to the ask.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal phrase that tells the reader a file is attached to the email.
entries.usage: Traditional in business and administrative email: *Please find attached the signed contract*. Many people now find it stiff or old-fashioned, and *I've attached…* or *Attached is…* sounds more modern. Both *please find attached the report* and *please find the report attached* are correct.
examples: **Please find attached** the signed lease and a copy of my ID.
**Please find attached** my résumé for the research assistant position.
My boss still writes "**please find attached**" even in two-line emails to the team.

drill.sentence: Dear Ms. Alvarez, {{please find attached}} the invoice for the March repairs.
drill.hint: old-fashioned formal way to point to the file (not *I've …* or *here is*)

entries.related: *I've attached* — modern and direct; *enclosed* — for paper letters; *see attached* — short and common, a little curt.

entries.term: I hope this email finds you well
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal opening line that politely wishes the reader well before the main message.
entries.usage: Very common in formal emails, especially to people you don't know well. Many readers find it a cliché, and it is widely joked about online, so with colleagues a direct start or *I hope you're well* is often better. It works best as a short first line, followed right away by the reason for writing.
examples: **I hope this email finds you well**. I'm writing to ask about the summer internship you posted.
My students start every email with "**I hope this email finds you well**," even when they're asking for an extension.
**I hope this email finds you well**, and that the move to Seattle went smoothly.

drill.sentence: Dear Dr. Okafor, {{I hope this email finds you well}}. I'm a second-year student interested in your research group.
drill.hint: the classic formal opener, seven words (not with *message* or *note*)

entries.related: *I hope you're well* — shorter and warmer; *I hope you had a great weekend* — casual and specific; *I'm reaching out because* — a direct start.

entries.label: short reply
entries.meaning: A one-word reply meaning *I have read this and will keep it in mind*.
entries.usage: Common in work chat and email to confirm you've received information or a correction. Alone it can sound cold or annoyed, especially after criticism, so many people add something: *Noted, thanks!* or *Noted, I'll fix that*. *Duly noted* is more formal and often sounds sarcastic.
examples: "The meeting moved to Room 204." "**Noted**, thanks!"
When I told my teenage son his curfew was eleven, he just said "**noted**" and went upstairs.
**Noted**: I'll use the new template for all client reports from now on.

drill.sentence: "Just so you know, the client prefers PDFs, not Word files." "{{Noted}}. I'll send PDFs from now on."
drill.hint: one-word reply: I've read it and will remember (not *understood*)

entries.related: *got it* — casual, very common; *understood* — slightly more formal; *duly noted* — formal, often sarcastic.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a question or statement that checks you have understood something correctly, or that prevents a misunderstanding.
entries.usage: Common in emails, meetings and customer service: *Just to clarify, do you need the report by Friday or Monday?* The word *just* keeps it polite and shows you're not challenging the other person. It can also gently correct a misunderstanding (*Just to clarify, I didn't approve the budget*).
examples: **Just to clarify**, are we meeting at the restaurant or at your place first?
**Just to clarify**, I'm not leaving the company; I'm moving to a different team.
I asked the pharmacist, "**Just to clarify**, should I take this with food or on an empty stomach?"

drill.sentence: {{Just to clarify}}, when you say "early next week," do you mean Monday or Tuesday?
drill.hint: checking that I understand correctly (not *to be clear* or *… to confirm*)

entries.related: *to be clear* — states your position firmly; *just to confirm* — checks a detail you think you know; *if I understand correctly* — more formal.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal request, usually at the end of an email, asking the reader to tell you what to do or how to proceed.
entries.usage: Common in business and administrative email, often as the last line after describing a problem. Alone it can sound curt or impatient, because it hands the reader a task without a thank-you; *Could you let me know how you'd like me to proceed?* is warmer. It is still normal in official, legal and shipping emails.
examples: The shipment arrived with two boxes damaged. **Please advise** whether we should accept it.
The patient's insurance won't cover the scan. **Please advise**.
My manager's emails always end with "**please advise**," which makes even small questions sound urgent.

drill.sentence: The venue says our deposit never arrived, but my bank shows it was paid. {{Please advise}}.
drill.hint: formal: tell me what I should do (not *let me know*)

entries.related: *let me know how to proceed* — warmer; *please confirm* — asks for a yes or no; *per my last email* — another phrase that can sound curt.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Means *as I already said in my previous email*; usually a polite-sounding way to say that the reader didn't read it or ignored it.
entries.usage: Famous as passive-aggressive office language: polite on the surface, but it signals irritation. Use it only when you really mean to make that point, and rarely with clients or managers. A neutral alternative is to restate the key point briefly (*Quick recap: the deadline is Friday*).
examples: **Per my last email**, the deadline is Friday, not Monday.
When my landlord wrote "**per my last email**," I knew he was annoyed that I'd asked again.
I almost wrote "**per my last email**" to the school, then softened it to "as I mentioned earlier."

drill.sentence: {{Per my last email}}, the forms must be signed by both parents, so we can't accept this one.
drill.hint: a pointed written way to say *I already told you this* (not *as I mentioned*)

entries.related: *as per my last email* — same, just as pointed; *as I mentioned* — milder; *per our conversation* — neutral reference to a talk; *friendly reminder* — can also sound pointed.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite thank-you to someone who has been waiting for you, for your reply or for a problem to be solved.
entries.usage: Common in customer service and work email, often instead of an apology: *Thanks for your patience while we fixed the issue*. It sounds more positive than *sorry for the delay* because it focuses on the reader, but if the delay was your fault, using both can be best. Use *with* for the person or thing and *while* for the period.
entries.pattern: thanks for your patience (with … / while …)
examples: **Thanks for your patience** while we sorted out the billing error; your refund is on its way.
The pilot announced, "**Thank you for your patience**; we should be cleared for takeoff shortly."
I know my replies have been slow this semester, so **thanks for your patience**.

drill.sentence: Our technician will arrive tomorrow between nine and noon. {{Thanks for your patience}} while we resolve this.
drill.hint: thank the customer for waiting calmly (not *… understanding*)

entries.related: *thanks for your understanding* — thanks for accepting a problem; *apologies for the delay* — focuses on your fault; *bear with me* — asks for patience in advance.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A chain of emails on one subject, made of the original message and all the replies to it.
entries.usage: Common in work talk: *I'll add you to the thread*, *It's buried somewhere in the thread*. Long threads with many people are a common complaint, and when one gets long, people often suggest a call instead. On Slack and forums, *thread* means a chain of replies to one message.
entries.pattern: on / in the (email) thread; add someone to the thread
examples: The decision is somewhere in that forty-message **email thread**, but good luck finding it.
My cousins started **an email thread** to plan Grandma's ninetieth birthday, and it now has two hundred replies.
Please reply on the original **email thread** so the whole committee can see the history.

drill.sentence: I can't find the budget numbers. Could you forward me {{the email thread}} where Sam explained them?
drill.hint: the whole series of replies on that subject (not *… chain*)

entries.related: *an email chain* — same; *reply all* — answer everyone on a thread; *a Slack thread* — replies to one chat message.

entries.label: verb (also noun)
entries.meaning: To send your reply to everyone who received the original email, not only to the sender.
entries.usage: Useful when the whole group needs your answer, but unnecessary reply-alls are a classic office annoyance, especially on large mailing lists. *Reply all* is the verb, *a reply-all* is the noun, and *a reply-all storm* is a chain of mass replies. Before you reply all, ask whether everyone really needs to see it.
examples: Please don't **reply all** to say thanks; there are three hundred people on this list.
Someone **replied all** asking to be removed, and soon the whole company was doing it.
My aunt accidentally **replied all** with her honest opinion of the wedding menu.

drill.sentence: If your answer affects everyone's schedule, {{reply all}} so the whole committee sees it.
drill.hint: answer the sender and everyone else on the email

entries.related: *reply* — answer only the sender; *cc* — send a copy to someone; *bcc* — send a hidden copy.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *for your information*: you are sharing something useful, and usually no action is needed.
entries.usage: Very common in email subject lines (*FYI: new parking rules*) and when forwarding something. In speech it is said as letters, and it can sound sharp, as in *FYI, I've been here since eight*. In formal emails, write *for your information* or *for your reference*.
examples: **FYI**, the office will close at three on Friday for the holiday.
I forwarded you the city's notice about street cleaning, just as an **FYI**.
"**FYI**, I've been waiting here for forty minutes," my friend texted when I was late again.

drill.sentence: No need to reply; this is just an {{FYI}} so you know the printer on the third floor is broken.
drill.hint: three-letter abbreviation for information that needs no action (not *update*)

entries.related: *a heads-up* — advance warning, often with something to prepare; *for your reference* — more formal; *PSA* — public service announcement, used jokingly.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *too long; didn't read*: a very short summary of a long text, or a comment that a text is too long.
entries.usage: Common online and in casual work messages, often at the top of a long email: *TL;DR: we're two weeks behind*. As a reply to someone else's text it can sound rude, but as a label for your own summary it is friendly. Americans usually say it as letters, *T-L-D-R*.
examples: **TL;DR**: the move is delayed by two weeks, but the budget is fine. Details below.
My friend's text was three screens long, so I asked for the **TL;DR**.
Many blog posts now start with a **TL;DR** box for readers in a hurry.

drill.sentence: The full report is forty pages, but here's the {{TL;DR}}: sales are up, and costs are flat.
drill.hint: internet abbreviation for a very short summary (not *short version* or *gist*)

entries.related: *the short version* — the spoken equivalent; *the bottom line* — the main conclusion; *an executive summary* — a formal summary at the start of a report.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *estimated time of arrival*; at work, also the expected time when something will be ready or done.
entries.usage: Common in travel, deliveries and work chat: *What's your ETA?* or *Any ETA on the fix?* Americans usually say it as letters, *E-T-A*. Asking for an ETA is a neutral, efficient way to ask when something will happen, though asking again and again can feel like pressure.
entries.pattern: What's your ETA? / an ETA on + task
examples: I'm stuck in traffic. My **ETA** is about twenty minutes, so start without me.
Do we have an **ETA** on the new laptops for the interns?
The app showed the plumber's **ETA** as 2:15, but he arrived at four.

drill.sentence: The website's been down for an hour. Does IT have an {{ETA}} for when it'll be back up?
drill.hint: an expected time — three letters (not *estimate*)

entries.related: *a timeline* — the planned schedule; *ASAP* — as soon as possible; *ETD* — estimated time of departure.

entries.label: phrase / abbreviation
entries.meaning: Away from work, for example on vacation or sick leave, and not reading or answering email; written *OOO* in calendars and chat.
entries.usage: Common in calendars, chat statuses and auto-replies: *I'm OOO next week*. In full sentences Americans usually say *out of the office* (*I'll be out of the office until Monday*) or just *out* (*I'm out Friday*). *An out-of-office* is the automatic reply your email sends while you're away.
examples: I'll be **out of the office** from December 20 to January 2 with limited access to email.
I'm **OOO** tomorrow for a doctor's appointment, but I'll check Slack at lunch.
I forgot to turn off my **out-of-office** message, so clients kept thinking I was on vacation.

drill.sentence: Kim's calendar shows her as {{out of office}} until Monday, so please ask Raj about the invoice instead.
drill.hint: away from work, as a calendar status (not *on vacation* or *away*)

entries.related: *on PTO* — on paid time off, US; *an auto-reply* — an automatic email response; *off the grid* — completely unreachable.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *paid time off*: the days off, such as vacation and sometimes sick days, that an employer pays you for.
entries.usage: Standard in American workplaces and HR: *I have five days of PTO left*, *I'm on PTO next week*. It is said as letters, *P-T-O*. British speakers say *annual leave* or *holiday*, and in British English *PTO* usually means *please turn over* on a printed page.
entries.pattern: on PTO; take / use / request PTO
examples: I'm saving my **PTO** for a two-week trip to Japan in the spring.
The new job offers unlimited **PTO**, but nobody seems to actually take it.
My manager approved my **PTO** request for the week of my daughter's surgery.

drill.sentence: I used all my {{PTO}} when the baby was born, so I'll have to work through the holidays.
drill.hint: paid days off, three letters (not *vacation days*)

entries.related: *vacation days* — plainer; *sick leave* — paid days off for illness; *annual leave* — the British term.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An unsolicited email sent to someone you have never met and have no connection with, often to ask for a job, a meeting or business.
entries.usage: Common in job searches, sales and academia: *I sent cold emails to three professors about a PhD position*. It is also a verb, *cold-email someone*. Because the reader owes you nothing, a good cold email is short, specific and polite.
entries.pattern: send a cold email (to someone); cold-email someone
examples: I sent **a cold email** to the author of the book, and to my surprise she replied the next day.
Most of the **cold emails** I get are from companies selling software I don't need.
She landed her first internship by **cold-emailing** twenty labs that worked on ocean currents.

drill.sentence: I didn't know anyone at the company, so I sent {{a cold email}} to the head of design and asked for fifteen minutes.
drill.hint: an unsolicited message to a total stranger (not just *a message*)

entries.related: *a warm intro* — an introduction from someone you both know; *a cold call* — the same idea by phone; *networking* — building professional contacts.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An introduction to someone made by a person you both already know, which makes them more likely to respond.
entries.usage: Common in American startup, business and job-search talk: *Could you give me a warm intro to your manager?* It contrasts with *a cold email*: the shared contact's trust makes a reply much more likely. The full form *warm introduction* is more neutral.
entries.pattern: give / make someone a warm intro (to someone)
examples: My former advisor gave me **a warm intro** to her colleague at the museum, and I got an interview the next week.
Investors rarely answer cold emails, so founders work hard to get **warm intros**.
A friend from my running club gave us **a warm intro** to a great family lawyer when we needed one.

drill.sentence: I'd love to meet your old boss, but a cold email won't get far. Could you make {{a warm intro}}?
drill.hint: an introduction through someone we both know — informal (not just *an introduction*)

entries.related: *a cold email* — contact with no introduction; *connect two people* — introduce them, informal; *a referral* — a recommendation, often for a job.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal request to ignore an earlier message, attachment or piece of information, usually because it was sent by mistake or is wrong.
entries.usage: Common in correction emails: *Please disregard my previous email*, or simply *Please disregard* as a subject line. It sounds neutral and professional, and adding the corrected information helps. In casual chat, *ignore that* or *never mind* is more natural.
entries.pattern: please disregard + my previous email / the attachment / this notice
examples: **Please disregard** the attachment in my last email; it was an old version of the schedule.
If you've already paid this bill, **please disregard** this notice.
The school's text said, "**Please disregard** the earlier message about the snow day; classes will run as usual."

drill.sentence: Sorry, I sent the wrong file. {{Please disregard}} it; the correct version is attached.
drill.hint: formal request to pay no attention to it (not *… ignore*)

entries.related: *ignore* — plainer; *never mind* — casual, for small corrections; *apologies for any confusion* — often follows a correction.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite apology after you sent a mistaken, unclear or contradictory message.
entries.usage: Common as the last line of a correction email, right after the corrected detail. *Any* keeps it light, because it doesn't assume the reader was actually confused. It is a little formal; *sorry for the mix-up* is the casual version.
examples: Correction: the meeting is at 3:00, not 2:00. **Apologies for any confusion**.
The school sent a second text with the right pickup time and **apologies for any confusion**.
I mixed up the two restaurants in my message, so **apologies for any confusion**: we're meeting at Luigi's.

drill.sentence: The earlier post had the wrong date for the bake sale; it's on Saturday. {{Apologies for any confusion}}.
drill.hint: a polite, verbless way to say sorry for the wrong date (not *sorry for …*)

entries.related: *sorry for the mix-up* — casual; *please disregard* — tells the reader to ignore an earlier message; *to clarify* — introduces the corrected information.

entries.label: fixed phrase
entries.meaning: With very little warning or time to prepare.
entries.usage: Common in requests, thanks and apologies: *Sorry to ask on such short notice*, *Thanks for coming in on short notice*. American English says *on short notice*; British English prefers *at short notice*. *Such* often strengthens it: *on such short notice*.
entries.pattern: on (such) short notice
examples: Thanks for covering my shift **on such short notice**; I owe you one.
The hotel couldn't find us a room **on short notice** during the festival.
The professor canceled the exam **on short notice** because of the storm.

drill.sentence: The plumber came {{on short notice}}, even though it was a Sunday morning.
drill.hint: with almost no warning — American preposition (not *right away*)

mistake.wrong: Thank you for helping us in such short notice.
mistake.right: Thank you for helping us on such short notice.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase takes *on* in American English (*at* in British English), never *in*.

entries.related: *at short notice* — the British form; *last-minute* — happening just before the deadline; *in advance* — the opposite, beforehand.

entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: Promptly and without unnecessary delay, within a reasonable or expected time.
entries.usage: Common in formal and administrative writing such as contracts, job ads, policies and complaints (*Invoices must be paid in a timely manner*). It sounds bureaucratic and doesn't say how much time is acceptable, so in normal emails a date (*by Friday*) or *promptly* is clearer. In speech it can sound stiff.
examples: Employees are expected to respond to customer complaints **in a timely manner**.
If the landlord doesn't make repairs **in a timely manner**, tenants can contact the city.
Several reviews praised the clinic's staff for returning calls **in a timely manner**.

drill.sentence: Our policy requires that all expense reports be submitted {{in a timely manner}}, ideally within thirty days of the trip.
drill.hint: without unnecessary delay — formal, bureaucratic (not *promptly*, *on time* or *… fashion*)

entries.related: *promptly* — shorter, clearer; *at your earliest convenience* — as soon as you can, formal; *in due course* — eventually, at the right time, formal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Needing attention or action soon, because it loses value or causes problems after a certain time or deadline.
entries.usage: Common in email subject lines and notices: *Time-sensitive: please sign by Friday*. It is more neutral and less alarming than *urgent*, and it explains that a deadline exists. It is usually hyphenated, especially before a noun (*a time-sensitive request*).
examples: This offer is **time-sensitive**, so please let us know by Friday whether you accept.
Some blood samples are **time-sensitive** and must reach the hospital lab within two hours.
Sorry to bother you on vacation, but this is **time-sensitive**: the bank needs your signature today.

drill.sentence: Please open this today: it's a {{time-sensitive}} request from the insurance company, and they close at five.
drill.hint: needing action before a deadline — hyphenated adjective (not *urgent*)

entries.related: *urgent* — needs action now, stronger; *pressing* — important and urgent; *a hard deadline* — a deadline that cannot move.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A deadline that cannot be moved, usually because something serious happens if it is missed.
entries.usage: Common in project planning and email, often to separate real deadlines from flexible targets: *Friday is a soft deadline, but the 15th is a hard deadline*. Calling a deadline *hard* tells people not to ask for an extension. Grant and conference deadlines, court filings and tax dates are typical examples.
entries.pattern: a hard deadline (vs. a soft deadline)
examples: The grant portal closes at 5 p.m. on the 15th, and that's **a hard deadline**: no exceptions.
The wedding is in June, so the dress fitting in May is **a hard deadline**.
We can be flexible on the draft, but the printer's **hard deadline** is Thursday at noon.

drill.sentence: The city won't accept late applications, so March 1 is {{a hard deadline}}; plan to submit a week early.
drill.hint: a cutoff that cannot move (not *a firm …* or *a strict …*)

entries.related: *a soft deadline* — a target that can move; *a firm deadline* — similar; *time-sensitive* — needing action soon.
